source_read: PDF, pp. 189-192 (all pages; Table 1 and Figures 1-2 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi)

claims.overstatement: Minor wording points. (1) 'suicides ... were left out': the paper excludes intentional (suicidal) drug overdoses; other suicides only as obvious lethal injuries. (2) 'at the one US centre that measured it': Hancock itself describes, second-hand, other US studies of the same question (11-13% of suspected drug deaths with no substance found and another cause; 75-80% correct without internal examination), so 'the one study read here' is safer. (3) The 'upper limit' is the editors' inference, valid within the 2,719 suspected deaths and only if toxicology-negative deaths would not have been put down to drugs; deaths not suspected with drugs present and another cause found (inside the 122) could also be misattributed without autopsy, so it is not an upper limit for all misattribution. (4) The 115 found 'in the other direction' were identified by toxicology in the absence of autopsy findings (by definition), not by the autopsy. The claim correctly avoids the paper's term 'false-positive rate' for 9.75% and does not present it as a count change.
claims.note: Every number from this source checked on the rendered pages: 33 counties, 2,354,038, 2016-2021, 2,956, 2,719, 265, 9.75%, 237, 115, 48.5% (editors' calculation, recomputed), Wilson intervals 8.7-10.9% and 42.2-54.9% (recomputed), sensitivity 95.52% and specificity 31.52% (printed and recomputed). Examples of non-drug causes match. The pathologist's conclusion as yardstick and the counting rule for illicit drugs are on p. 192. The split of the 265 by toxicology result is indeed not reported. Reporting issue: running text (p. 190) gives 2,569/387 as suspected/not suspected, contradicting Table 1.

anchors.extracted: Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist Regional Autopsy Center serves 33 counties of western North Carolina (total population 2,354,038) and kept performing standard autopsies on suspected drug-related deaths through 2021, while other medical examiner/coroner offices had adopted external viewing with collection of toxicology specimens.

Case files with a standard medicolegal autopsy at the centre, 2016-2021. Excluded: decedents under 18, deaths from obvious lethal injury, and deaths from intentional (suicidal) prescription or illicit drug overdose (excluded because already labelled intentional at referral, biasing toward true positives, and because many did not meet the study criteria). Suicides by other means are excluded only insofar as they are obvious lethal injuries.

Pre-autopsy suspicion came from the preliminary report of death, compiled by the centre's medicolegal death investigators from county medical examiners with the same standardized questions the study used. Criteria for a likely drug-related death: drug paraphernalia at the scene (needles, syringes, cut straws, burnt foil, baggies with residue etc.), current or prior substance use disorder, prior overdoses. How the criteria were combined is not stated.

Point-of-care urine immunoassay screens were not used; specimens went to a forensic toxicology laboratory that screened for over-the-counter, prescription and illicit drugs (GC-MS, GC-NPD, targeted LC-high-resolution MS), with screen positives confirmed and quantified by LC-MS-MS.

False positive = high suspicion at referral but toxicology negative, OR illicit substances present with significant non-toxicological findings explaining death; false negative = very low or no suspicion at referral but toxicology showed drug toxicity as the cause with no significant autopsy findings. 'False-positive rate' = FP / all suspected cases (1 minus positive predictive value, not 1 minus specificity); 'false-negative rate' = FN / all toxicology-confirmed overdoses; authors note the definitions are not universal.

6,248 autopsy files reviewed, 2,956 included. Table 1: suspected before autopsy 2,719 (final cause drug-related 2,454, not drug-related 265); not suspected 237 (drug-related 115, not 122); final totals 2,569 drug-related, 387 not. Printed: sensitivity 95.52%, specificity 31.52%, false-negative rate 4.48%, false-positive rate 9.75%. Recomputed: 265/2,719 = 9.75% (Wilson 95% CI 8.7-10.9%); 115/237 = 48.5% (42.2-54.9%); 2,454/2,569 = 95.52%; 122/387 = 31.52%; 115/2,569 = 4.48%. The running text calls 2,569 and 387 the numbers suspected and not suspected at referral: these are the table's final-finding column totals and contradict its rows (2,719 and 237) and the TP/FP/FN/TN counts; the claim correctly follows the table.

Authors: pre-autopsy suspicion caught more than 95% of drug deaths (sensitivity); the 9.75% are cases that could have been misclassified as drug-related if only investigation, toxicology and external examination had been done. The autopsy found Adelson class I (catastrophic) processes, e.g. pulmonary emboli, ruptured gastric ulcer, ruptured berry aneurysm (no stimulants in the body), compressive subdural haematoma with manner homicide. The 265 are nowhere split by toxicology result (none found vs drugs present).

Authors say their results support a correct determination from scene investigation, external examination and comprehensive toxicology in a majority of cases; second-hand they describe a similar US study (11-13% of suspected drug deaths with no substance found on toxicology and another cause) and a study in which three pathologists given history, scene, external findings and toxicology got cause and manner right in 75-80% without internal examination.

The cause of death given by the assigned forensic pathologist was taken as correct (no independent reference standard); illicit drugs present were taken as at least contributing unless a class I natural or traumatic process was found; sample limited to western North Carolina.

claims.overstatement: 'some with drugs present and some with none found' restates the paper's definition of a false positive (toxicology negative, or illicit drugs present with another sufficient finding); the paper never reports that both kinds occurred or how many of each. Suggest 'which by the paper's definition include deaths with no drug found and deaths with drugs present but another sufficient cause (the split is not reported)'. Hancock reports no drug concentrations at all, so it bears on presence versus cause, not on what a level shows; it should not be read as illustrating 'a level that looks high'.
claims.note: Numbers 265/2,719 (9.75%) and 115/237 (48.5%, recomputed) correct; the counting rule (illicit drug present = at least contributing unless an Adelson class I process) is stated as a limitation on p. 192. Pathologists assigned the final cause after toxicology, consistent with the claim's remark that certifiers knew the results.

Confirmed: the verbal definition (negative preliminary findings that are true overdose deaths) gives 115/237, the formula and printed value 115/2,569.
Confirmed; see 'missed' on how far the upper bound reaches.
2019 national value 62,172 in Figure 1 (300 dpi) against 70,630 in Smiley-McDonald et al. (p. 542); 2017 70,237 matches Davis et al. (p. 152).

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, moderate, as a description of this series; domains 4 (no) and 7 (unclear) are the main weaknesses.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the 9.75% is presented as misclassification without autopsy, and sensitivity as prediction accuracy.

missed: The upper bound holds only within the 2,719 suspected deaths. Deaths not suspected that had drugs present but another cause found at autopsy (inside the 122 'true negatives') could also be put down to drugs without autopsy, so 9.75% does not bound all misattribution (refine reporting issue 3 and cannot_establish).

p. 191, Discussion 1st paragraph: the authors themselves say scene investigation, external examination and comprehensive toxicology gave a correct determination in a majority of cases. This tempers the Conclusions and could be added to the interpretation gap.
